\title{\psmcrs: fast PSMC inference that reproduces the reference implementation}
\author{Yufan Han\\[2pt]
  \small School of Life Sciences, Fudan University, Shanghai, China\\

\begin{abstract}
\noindent The pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC) infers the history of effective population size from a single diploid genome and is one of the most widely used methods of population genomics. Its reference implementation, the C program psmc, runs on one thread, which makes bootstraps and large cohorts slow. We present \psmcrs{}, a reimplementation of PSMC in Rust that fits the same model as C psmc. On \EoneGenomes{} simulated and \RealGenomes{} real genomes, the two programs' estimates of population size differed by at most \AgreeMaxPct{} over the time range each genome informs. On the simulated genomes, their histories were at least \EoneFoldMin{} times closer to each other than either was to the true history. On a simulated genome of 30 chromosomes of 100~Mb, \psmcrs{} was \EthreeSpeedOne{} times as fast as C psmc on one thread and \EthreeSpeedThirty{} times as fast on 30 threads, and it used at most \EthreeRsMemThirty{}~MB of memory, against C psmc's \EthreeCMem{}~MB. Its results were byte-identical on any number of threads. Fitting all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated high-coverage genomes of the 1000 Genomes Project took \psmcrs{} \EsevenRsCoreHours{} core-hours, where C psmc would have needed about \EsevenCCoreHoursAll{}. \psmcrs{} also reads VCF and multihetsep files, accounts for partly callable bins, and runs PSMC's block bootstrap in parallel. It is open source under the MIT license, and the pipeline behind every result, with the inputs and fits of the \EsevenGenomes{} genomes, is openly available.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Introduction}

The pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent \citep[PSMC;][]{li2011} infers how the effective size (\Ne) of a population changed over time from the two genome copies of a single diploid individual. Along the genome, the time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) of the two copies changes at recombination events. PSMC treats this time as the hidden state of a hidden Markov model whose observations are short bins of sequence, each heterozygous or homozygous, and fits a piecewise-constant history of \Ne{} by expectation--maximization (EM). Because it needs only one unphased genome, PSMC has been applied to modern and archaic humans \citep{li2011,prufer2014,mallick2016} and to a wide range of other species \citep{nadachowska2016,hilgers2025}, and it remains the baseline for newer coalescent hidden Markov models \citep{schiffels2014,terhorst2017,cousins2025,terhorst2025}.

PSMC's reference implementation, the C program \texttt{psmc} \citep{psmcC}, runs on one thread. Twenty-five EM iterations on a 3~Gb genome take more than an hour, a bootstrap multiplies that time by its number of replicates, and population resources such as the high-coverage 1000 Genomes data \citep{byrskabishop2022} now hold thousands of genomes. Other programs port PSMC to other languages and toolkits \citep{psmcr,psmcpython,smckit} or extend its model \citep{schiffels2020,liu2022,cousins2024,cousins2025}. Methods that combine many genomes or fit a richer model answer other questions. To replace C psmc, a faster program must keep its estimator and reproduce its results, so that new curves remain comparable with the many PSMC curves already published. The native PSMC of smckit has been checked against C psmc on one chromosome \citep{smckit}; we are not aware of a program shown to reproduce C psmc's fits of whole genomes on the same inputs while running substantially faster than C psmc.

Here we present \psmcrs{}, a reimplementation of PSMC in Rust. We show that it reproduces C psmc's fits of simulated and real genomes. It is an order of magnitude faster than C psmc on one thread and, on genomes of many sequences, two orders of magnitude faster on many threads; it needs a fraction of the memory and gives results that do not depend on the number of threads. We then fit all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated high-coverage genomes of the 1000 Genomes Project, and release their inputs and fits.

\section*{Results}

\subsection*{\psmcrs{} fits the PSMC model as C psmc does}

\psmcrs{} fits the PSMC model of \citet{li2011} as C psmc 0.6.5 implements it: the same discretization of time, the same transition and emission probabilities, the same parameter patterns and starting point, and EM on the same objective (Methods). It reads C psmc's input format, \texttt{psmcfa}; VCF files, either all-sites consensus calls or variant calls with a mask of callable sites; and the multihetsep files of MSMC \citep{schiffels2014}. It writes the fitted model as JSON and as an HTML report and, on request, in C psmc's \texttt{.psmc} format, which C psmc's \texttt{psmc\_plot.pl} draws. With the settings of C psmc's documentation, this command fits a human genome for 25 EM iterations on eight threads:
\begin{verbatim}
psmc-rs NA12878.psmcfa.gz NA12878.json 25 --pattern "4+25*2+4+6" --t-max 15 \
    --tr-ratio 5 --mu 1.25e-8 --gen-years 29 --threads 8 --psmc-out NA12878.psmc
\end{verbatim}
\psmcrs{} differs from C psmc in four ways (Methods). First, it processes the sequences of a genome (its chromosomes or scaffolds) in parallel, each on one thread. Second, its maximization step (M-step) runs L-BFGS to convergence, within bounds on the parameters, where C psmc runs a Hooke--Jeeves search. Third, it counts the last bin of each sequence, which C psmc leaves out of its expected emission counts. Fourth, when the input records how many of a bin's bases are callable, that is, could be genotyped, it weights the bin by that number.

\subsection*{\psmcrs{} reproduces C psmc}

\label{fig:agree}
\end{figure}

We fitted both programs, with the same inputs and settings, to \EoneGenomes{} simulated genomes of \EoneGenomeMb{}~Mb, \EoneReps{} under each of \EoneModelsW{} demographic models, and to \RealGenomes{} real genomes: \EtwoTurtlesW{} turtles and \EsevenDefault{} human genomes of the 1000 Genomes Project, two per population, which we call the comparison subset (experiments E1, E2 and E7; Methods). We compared the fits over each genome's informative window, the times between the 1\% and 99\% quantiles of the pairwise coalescence time; outside it, the data say little about \Ne{}. As the difference between two fits we use $\Delta$, the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of one fit's $\log_{10}\Ne$ against the other's, interval by interval over this window (Methods). On every genome, $\Delta$ was at most \EtwoRsCRmseMax{} (Table~\ref{tab:agreement}, Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}). Across all \AgreeIntervals{} intervals in the windows of these \AgreeGenomes{} genomes, the two programs' \Ne{} differed by a median of \AgreeMedianAbs{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ and by at most \AgreeMaxAbs{}, that is, by at most \AgreeMaxPct{}.

This difference is far smaller than the error of the method itself. On the simulated genomes, $\Delta$ ranged from \EoneRsCRmseMin{} to \EoneRsCRmseMax{} and was at least \EoneFoldMin{} times smaller than either program's error relative to the true history; the median $\Delta$ was \EoneFoldMedian{} times smaller than \psmcrs{}'s median error (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}e). The two programs' errors were equal to three decimals, from a mean RMSE of \EoneConstantTruthRs{} for the constant-size model to \EoneBottleneckTruthRs{} for the bottleneck model (Table~S1). The difference is also about \DiagOverCBuildsW{} times C psmc's own numerical noise. On the simulated genomes, the median $\Delta$ was \DiagMedianDefault{}, against a median of \DiagCBuildsMedian{} between C psmc's own fits on two platforms (gcc without floating-point contraction on x86-64, Apple clang with fused multiply-adds on arm64; Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}e, row `C psmc on two platforms'; Supplementary Note~1, section~9). Finally, it is far smaller than the sampling uncertainty of a fit: on the turtles and NA12878, the median width of \psmcrs{}'s bootstrap 95\% band was at least \EtwoBandOverDeltaMin{} times $\Delta$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}c, d).

The two programs compute the same likelihood; their small differences arise during the EM iterations. From the shared starting point, their first expectation steps (E-steps) gave log-likelihoods that agreed at about the rounding of the six decimals C psmc prints (a relative \EoneLoglikeFirstRelMax{}). In both programs the log-likelihood never decreased from one iteration to the next, and the two programs' log-likelihoods differed by at most \EoneSoneDiffMax{} units after any iteration (Fig.~S1). A diagnostic on the simulated genomes (Methods) traced the differences mostly to the last bin of each sequence, not to the M-step's optimizer. Leaving that bin out of \psmcrs{}'s expected emission counts, as C psmc does, lowered the median $\Delta$ from \DiagMedianDefault{} to \DiagMedianLastBin{}, below C psmc's own noise. It brought the curves closer to C psmc's in \DiagLastBinCloser{} of the \EoneGenomes{} genomes; the other \DiagLastBinOtherW{} were already within that noise. Replacing L-BFGS with C psmc's Hooke--Jeeves search barely changed the median (\DiagMedianHookeJeeves{}). Each sequence has one last bin, so the difference should grow with the number of sequences: among the turtles and NA12878, $\Delta$ was smallest for NA12878, with \EtwoHumanSequences{} sequences, and largest for the turtle \textit{Pelusios castaneus}, with \EtwoTurtleSeqMax{} (Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}c--e). It also depends on the history: the simulated genomes, of ten sequences each, reached up to \EoneRsCRmseMax{}.

Both programs share PSMC's weakness at the most recent times, about which one genome says little. With the pattern used here, a single parameter, the first free $\lambda$ (a size relative to $N_0$; Methods), sets \Ne{} in the four most recent time intervals. In one of the \EoneGenomes{} simulated genomes, this parameter ran away in both programs, outside the informative window: to \psmcrs{}'s upper bound of $10^4$ and, in C psmc, which has no bound, to \EoneRunawayC{}. The turtles' curves show recent peaks of \Ne{} (one shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}d), artefacts of this grouping that \citet{hilgers2025} found in many published PSMC curves. Giving the four most recent intervals two or four free $\lambda$s instead of one removed the peaks in all \EtwoSplitFitsW{} fits and raised the log-likelihood by \EtwoSplitGainMin{} to \EtwoSplitGainMax{} units.

\subsection*{\psmcrs{} is fast and deterministic}

\centering

\label{fig:perf}

To measure speed, we timed both programs on simulated constant-size genomes of 1, 3, 10 and 30 chromosomes of 100~Mb, each run alone on an exclusive node, with \EthreeRepeatsW{} repeats on \EthreeNodesW{} nodes (experiment E3; Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}a, b, Table~\ref{tab:timing}, Methods). On one thread, 25 EM iterations on the \EthreeBigMb{}~Mb genome took \psmcrs{} \EthreeRsOneWall{}~s (\EthreeRsOneMin{} minutes) and C psmc \EthreeCWall{}~s (\EthreeCMin{} minutes): \psmcrs{} was \EthreeSpeedOne{} times as fast (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}a), and \EthreeSpeedOneMin{} to \EthreeSpeedOneMax{} times as fast at every size (Table~\ref{tab:timing}). With the sequences in parallel, it was \EthreeSpeedEight{}, \EthreeSpeedSixteen{} and \EthreeSpeedThirty{} times as fast as C psmc on 8, 16 and 30 threads (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}a, Table~\ref{tab:timing}), and fitted the \EthreeBigMb{}~Mb genome in \EthreeRsWallThirty{}~s. Its parallel efficiency, its speed-up over its own one-thread time divided by the number of threads, was \EthreeEffMin{} to \EthreeEffMax{} on 2 to 30 threads (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}a, grey line).

Because each sequence runs on one thread, a genome's longest sequence bounds the speed-up. One 100~Mb chromosome took \EthreeChromWallMin{} to \EthreeChromWallMax{}~s on 1, 8 and 30 threads alike (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}a, dotted line); the 30-thread speed-up holds because this genome has 30 chromosomes of equal length. A human genome's speed-up on many threads is bounded in the same way, by its chromosome~1 (\EsevenLongestMb{}~Mb).

\psmcrs{} also needed far less memory than C psmc: \EthreeRsMemOne{}~MB on one thread and \EthreeRsMemThirty{}~MB on 30, against \EthreeCMem{}~MB (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}b). C psmc keeps the forward and backward vectors of every bin of a sequence, and its E-step takes time quadratic in the number of states. \psmcrs{} keeps the forward vectors only at checkpoints and recomputes the rest, and for models of up to 256 states its E-step takes time linear in the number of states \citep[Methods;][]{harris2014}.

\psmcrs{}'s results do not depend on the number of threads. For each genome size, all its fitted models, from every thread count, repeat and node, were byte-identical (\EthreeDetRsTotal{} fits in all), as were C psmc's (\EthreeDetCTotal{} fits). The bootstrap runs of the turtles and NA12878, on \EtwoBootThreads{} threads, refitted each genome's one-thread fit exactly. NA12878's bootstrap, run with the same seed on \EtwoBootThreads{} and on \EsevenBootThreads{} threads, wrote \EsevenBootFilesIdentical{} of its \EsevenBootFiles{} files byte for byte the same. Across platforms, results differ only slightly. We refitted the \EoneGenomes{} simulated genomes with a build from the same source code on a laptop with another processor architecture, operating system and math library. No parameter differed from the cluster's fits by more than a relative \XpParamRelMax{}. The laptop's curves were within a $\Delta$ of \XpRsRmseMax{} of the cluster's, a median of \XpRatioCMedian{} times closer than C psmc's own fits on the same two platforms (Supplementary Note~1, section~9).

\subsection*{Partly callable bins, bootstrap and decoding}

\psmcrs{} can also account for bins that are only partly callable. C psmc's input is made by \texttt{fq2psmcfa}, which marks a 100~bp bin missing only when more than 90\% of its bases are uncallable. A bin with fewer uncallable bases is fitted as if all its bases had been observed, which biases PSMC's estimates \citep{lipson2015,nadachowska2016}. When the input records how many of a bin's bases are callable, as a VCF with its callable mask does, \psmcrs{} weights the bin by that number (Methods), as recent coalescent hidden Markov models do \citep{cousins2024,cousins2025}. Inputs that record no callable counts, such as \texttt{psmcfa} files, are fitted with C psmc's model unchanged.

We tested the weighting on simulated genomes with 10\% or 30\% of positions uncallable, either in short runs, which leave many bins partly callable, or in long runs, which empty whole bins (experiment E4). With short runs, taking every called (non-missing) bin as full, as \texttt{fq2psmcfa} does, underestimated the scaled mutation rate $\theta$, and with it every size and time, by \EfourDispTenFqTheta{} or \EfourDispThirtyFqTheta{}. The weighted fit underestimated it by only \EfourDispTenAutoTheta{} or \EfourDispThirtyAutoTheta{} (Fig.~S2). Multihetsep files record how many sites are callable between two segregating sites, but not which, so \psmcrs{} takes their called bins as full by default. With 30\% of positions uncallable, their fits underestimated $\theta$ by \EfourDispThirtyMhsTheta{} with short runs and \EfourClusThirtyMhsTheta{} with long ones; a VCF read without its mask, by \EfourDispThirtyNomaskTheta{} and \EfourClusThirtyNomaskTheta{}.

\psmcrs{} runs PSMC's block bootstrap in parallel, each replicate drawing from its own random stream, so that a seed gives the same replicates on any number of threads. In a calibration study of one bottleneck model (experiment E5), the bootstrap's 95\% bands held the mean of independent fits at, on average, \EfiveFiftyCovMean{} of the times in the informative window with blocks of 50~Mb and \EfiveFiveCovMean{} with blocks of 5~Mb, but the true history at only \EfiveFiftyCov{} and \EfiveFiveCov{} (Fig.~S3). The bands measure the sampling variation of an estimate, not PSMC's bias.

Read from a VCF with no uncallable positions, a genome gives the same bins as its \texttt{psmcfa} and the same fit, bit for bit (experiment E6); with a callable mask, its partly callable bins are weighted, as above. From a multihetsep file, which ends at each sequence's last heterozygous site and places uncallable sites approximately, the fits differed from the \texttt{psmcfa} fits by a $\Delta$ of at most \EsixMhsRmseMax{}. It also decodes the posterior distribution of the TMRCA in every bin. In a simulated genome, the central 95\% of this distribution held the true TMRCA in \EsixDecodeCov{} of its bins; we did not compare this decoding with C psmc's. \psmcrs{} also checks every input before fitting it (\opt{psmc-rs qc}).

\subsection*{\EsevenGenomes{} human genomes}

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\makebox[\linewidth][c]{\includegraphics[width=183mm]{E7/figures/fig7_1000_genomes.pdf}}
\caption{\textbf{Population size histories of all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated individuals in the high-coverage 1000 Genomes data, each genome fitted by \psmcrs{} (E7).} (a) The median over each superpopulation's genomes. (b--f) One superpopulation each: its genomes (faint lines, which merge into a soft band where they agree), the median over each of its populations' genomes (\EsevenPerPopMin{} to \EsevenPerPopMax{} genomes per population; 1000 Genomes population codes; *, admixed) and, in grey, the other four superpopulations' medians from a. Medians are pointwise, at each time of a common grid, and span the cohort's informative window, from \EsevenWindowLoKy{} thousand to \EsevenWindowHiMy{} million years ago: the medians over genomes of each genome's 1\% and 99\% quantiles of the pairwise coalescence time. Pale: PSMC's first free $\lambda$, a single parameter for the four most recent intervals, which one genome constrains poorly. Each median is pale until nine in ten of its genomes have passed the span of their first free $\lambda$; each genome starts where its own first free $\lambda$ ends, and each grey median where it turns full in a. The fits are of the \texttt{psmcfa} inputs, which take every called bin as full; weighting bins by their callable bases raised the curves of the comparison subset almost uniformly, by a median of \EsevenRouteShiftMedian{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ (Results). $\mu=\EsevenMu$ per bp per generation, $g=\EsevenG$ years.}
\label{fig:kg}
\end{figure}

To show what this speed makes possible, we fitted \psmcrs{} to all \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated individuals of the high-coverage 1000 Genomes data \citep{byrskabishop2022}: \EsevenPops{} populations of \EsevenPerPopMin{} to \EsevenPerPopMax{} individuals, sequenced to a median depth of \EsevenDepth{}$\times$ (experiment E7; Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}). From the joint-called VCFs we made one \texttt{psmcfa} file per genome, with the strict accessibility mask \citep{kgp2015} and with every position whose record failed the callset's filters set missing (Methods). For NA12878, the heterozygous single-nucleotide variants from which this input was made matched Genome in a Bottle's benchmark \citep{zook2019,wagner2022} with a precision of \EsevenGiabPrecision{} and a recall of \EsevenGiabRecall{}.

Fitting one genome per thread on a shared node, \psmcrs{} took a median of \EsevenRsFitMin{} minutes per genome (Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}c) and \EsevenRsCoreHours{} core-hours for the cohort. C psmc, run the same way in the same job on the \EsevenDefault{} genomes of the comparison subset, took a median of \EsevenCFitMin{} minutes per genome, which would make about \EsevenCCoreHoursAll{} core-hours for the cohort. On these \EsevenDefault{} genomes, $\Delta$ between the two programs was \EsevenRsCRmseMin{} to \EsevenRsCRmseMax{} (Table~\ref{tab:agreement}).

The histories have the features of published single-genome PSMC analyses of human genomes \citep[Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}a;][]{li2011,prufer2014,mallick2016}. The median curves of the four superpopulations outside Africa fell to minima of \EsevenNonAfrMinNeLo{} to \EsevenNonAfrMinNeHi{} between \EsevenNonAfrMinKyLo{} and \EsevenNonAfrMinKyHi{} thousand years ago, whereas the African median fell only to \EsevenAfrMinNe{}. From \EsevenConvergeKy{} thousand years ago to the end of the window, \EsevenWindowHiMy{} million years ago, the five superpopulations' medians were within 20\% of one another.

Within each superpopulation, the population medians differed most over the span of the first free $\lambda$ (drawn pale in Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}), which one genome constrains poorly. There, the largest difference between two populations was \EsevenPopSpreadRecentLo{} to \EsevenPopSpreadRecentHi{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$, depending on the superpopulation. When we split the first free $\lambda$ into four, in one genome per population, the four values spanned a median of \EsevenSplitSpanMedian{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$: the single $\lambda$ averages over sizes that, fitted separately, differ more than tenfold, though each of the four is itself poorly constrained. After the first free $\lambda$, the population medians stayed close (Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}b--f). From its end to \EsevenPopCutKy{} thousand years ago, through the bottleneck and the rise after it, the highest and the lowest differed by a median over time of \EsevenPopSpreadMidMedLo{} to \EsevenPopSpreadMidMedHi{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$, depending on the superpopulation, and by at most \EsevenPopSpreadMidLo{} to \EsevenPopSpreadMidHi{} at any time. At older times, this median was at most \EsevenPopSpreadOldMed{} (largest single value, \EsevenPopSpreadOldMax{}). In East Asia, Europe and South Asia, the larger differences were brief: they fell where the populations' steps fell at slightly different times. Individual genomes were close too: after the first free $\lambda$, the middle 80\% of a superpopulation's genomes spanned a median of \EsevenIndivSpreadLo{} to \EsevenIndivSpreadHi{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$ outside the admixed Americas (Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}b--f).

Fitting the \EsevenDefault{} genomes of the comparison subset from their VCFs, with each bin weighted by its callable bases, raised the scaled mutation rate by a median of \EsevenThetaShift{} over their \texttt{psmcfa} fits. This is close to the \EsevenThetaExpected{} expected if $\theta$ scales with the callable bases: a median of \EsevenMissingShare{} of the bases in called bins were uncallable. The VCF fits lay almost uniformly above the \texttt{psmcfa} fits: interval by interval, by a median of \EsevenRouteShiftMedian{} in $\log_{10}\Ne$, with a median SD of \EsevenRouteShapeMedian{} around that shift (Methods).

The Project's own PSMC release holds only the output of fits made from the low-coverage (mean 7.4$\times$), imputed genotypes of the same individuals, and from high-coverage genomes of only 26 individuals \citep{kgp2015,kgpPsmc}. Here, every genome was fitted from its high-coverage sequence, and the \texttt{psmcfa} inputs and the fits of all \EsevenGenomes{} genomes are released as a resource, with the provenance of every fit (Data availability).

\section*{Discussion}

\psmcrs{} reproduces C psmc's fits. On the same inputs, its histories differ from C psmc's by far less than the method's own error and than the sampling uncertainty of a fit. Most of the remaining difference comes from one bookkeeping choice, the last bin of each sequence: with that bin left out, as C psmc leaves it out, the two programs differ about as little as C psmc's own fits on two platforms. Analyses of inputs like these can therefore move to \psmcrs{}, and published PSMC analyses can be repeated or extended with it, without their conclusions changing because of the program. We tested one pattern of parameters and 25 EM iterations, which do not reach convergence (Fig.~S1), on genomes of up to \EtwoTurtleSeqMax{} sequences. In Tasmanian devils, PSMC curves changed little with assembly quality \citep{patton2019}. Among the four genomes of E2, however, the difference between the two programs grew with the number of sequences, so fits of highly fragmented assemblies are worth comparing with C psmc's.

\psmcrs{} is an order of magnitude faster than C psmc on one thread and, on genomes of many sequences, two orders of magnitude faster on many threads. It needs a small fraction of C psmc's memory and gives the same results on any number of threads. For one genome, threads cut the wait. For a cohort or a bootstrap, which run many fits side by side, the speed per core and the smaller memory count: the \EsevenGenomes{} genomes took \EsevenRsCoreHours{} core-hours, where C psmc would have needed about \EsevenCCoreHoursAll{}.

\psmcrs{} keeps PSMC's model, and with it PSMC's limits. One genome says little about the last few thousand generations, where the first free $\lambda$ can run away; \psmcrs{} bounds it and warns when it does. Ancestral population structure can produce changes in a single-genome curve that are not changes in size \citep{mazet2016,cousins2025}, and methods that combine many genomes, such as MSMC2 \citep{schiffels2020}, SMC++ \citep{terhorst2017} or PHLASH \citep{terhorst2025}, resolve recent times better. The bootstrap measures sampling variation, not these biases (Fig.~S3). Finally, because \psmcrs{} parallelizes across sequences, a genome assembled into a few long sequences gains less from many threads than one assembled into many.

\psmcrs{} does not replace methods for many genomes; it makes the single-genome reference fast and reproducible.

\FloatBarrier
\section*{Methods}

\subsection*{Model}

\psmcrs{} fits the model of \citet{li2011} with the conventions of C psmc 0.6.5-r74 \citep{psmcC}. Time is measured in units of $2N_0$ generations and divided into $n+1$ intervals $[t_k,t_{k+1})$, with $t_k=\alpha(e^{\beta k}-1)$ for $k=0,\dots,n-1$, $\beta=\ln(1+t_{\max}/\alpha)/n$, $\alpha=0.1$, $t_n=t_{\max}$ and $t_{n+1}$ a large value standing for infinity (1,000, as in C psmc). The population size in interval $k$ is $\lambda_kN_0$. The free parameters are the scaled mutation rate $\theta$ and recombination rate $\rho$ per bin, $t_{\max}$, and the free $\lambda$s, each spanning consecutive intervals according to a pattern: \opt{4+25*2+4+6} has 64 intervals and 28 free $\lambda$s, the first spanning the four most recent intervals. The initial distribution, the transition probabilities and the expected coalescence time $\bar t_k$ in each interval are computed exactly as C psmc computes them (\psmcrs{}'s code is a line-by-line port of its \texttt{psmc\_update\_hmm}). A bin of $s$ bases is missing (N) if more than 90\% of its bases are uncallable, as in \texttt{fq2psmcfa}; otherwise it is heterozygous (K) if any of its callable sites is heterozygous, and homozygous (T) if none is. The emission probabilities are $e_T(k)=e^{-\theta\bar t_k}$, $e_K(k)=1-e_T(k)$ and $e_N(k)=1$. Sizes and times are scaled with a mutation rate $\mu$ per bp per generation, the bin size $s$ and a generation time $g$: $N_0=\theta/(4\mu s)$, $\Ne=\lambda_kN_0$, and a time $t$ is $2N_0tg$ years.

When the input records how many of a bin's $s$ bases are callable, $c$, \psmcrs{} uses
\begin{equation}
P(T\mid k,c)=e_T(k)^{c/s}=e^{-\theta\bar t_k c/s},\qquad P(K\mid k,c)=1-P(T\mid k,c),
\end{equation}
the probability that $c$ callable bases hold no heterozygous site under the Poisson bin likelihood of PSMC+ and cobraa \citep{cousins2024,cousins2025}, restricted to PSMC's binary observations (\opt{--bin-callable auto}, the default). Full bins, and inputs without counts, are fitted with C psmc's model. A VCF read with a callable mask gives $c$ as $s$ minus the bin's positions outside the mask, inside a negative mask, at records that failed the callset's filters, with a missing or partial genotype, or in the reference span of a heterozygous variant that is not a single-nucleotide variant. A multihetsep file gives only the number of callable sites between two of its rows; \psmcrs{} places the uncallable ones at the start of each such stretch, and \opt{--bin-callable auto} takes the bins that result as full.

\subsection*{Inference}

\paragraph{E-step.} The forward--backward algorithm runs in double precision on each sequence, with the forward vector normalized at every bin; the log-likelihood is the sum of the logarithms of the normalizers. To bound memory, the forward vector is kept every 128 bins and the vectors between these checkpoints are recomputed, to the same bits, during the backward pass. For models of up to 256 states the forward and backward passes take time linear in the number of states, from the rank-one structure of PSMC's transition matrix \citep{harris2014}. So do the expected transition counts, for models of any size: below and above the diagonal, a transition probability is the product of a factor of its row and a factor of its column, so C psmc's objective needs the counts only summed over the rows and columns of each triangle and over the diagonal, and the E-step adds these up from prefix and suffix sums at every bin. C psmc's \texttt{.psmc} output also reports the objective less its largest value over all models (its \texttt{QD} line), which needs every count; \psmcrs{}'s leaves that line out. The expected emission counts include the last bin of every sequence, which C psmc leaves out of them. On x86-64 processors with AVX2 and FMA, \psmcrs{} chooses kernels compiled for them when it starts, and portable kernels otherwise; on aarch64 it uses NEON kernels. The JSON output and the HTML report record which kernels ran.

\paragraph{M-step.} \psmcrs{} maximizes C psmc's objective, the expected complete-data log-likelihood of the transitions and emissions, over all free parameters with L-BFGS \citep{liu1989}. It uses a memory of 20, an Armijo line search and gradients from a hand-written adjoint, on logits within the bounds $\theta,\rho\in[10^{-12},10]$ per bin, $t_{\max}\in[1,200]$ and $\lambda\in[10^{-6},10^4]$. It stops when, in each of two consecutive iterations, the objective improved by at most a relative $10^{-13}$ and the next quasi-Newton step predicts no larger improvement, or when its line search finds no improvement; before stopping, it restarts from fresh estimates of the curvature, up to three times, if they predict a larger improvement. It also stops after 1,000 iterations. C psmc instead uses a Hooke--Jeeves direct search \citep{hooke1961} on unbounded parameters. EM starts, as C psmc's does, from $\theta_0=-\ln(1-K/L)$, with $K$ the heterozygous and $L$ the non-missing bins (with callable counts, the root of $\sum_i(1-e^{-\theta_0c_i/s})=K$), $\rho_0=\theta_0/r$ (\opt{--tr-ratio}, 4 by default), $t_{\max}$ (\opt{--t-max}, 15) and every $\lambda=1$.

\paragraph{Parallelism and determinism.} The E-step and the log-likelihood run in parallel over work items, contiguous groups of whole sequences whose grouping depends only on the number of sequences; partial sums are merged in the order of the items, so they do not depend on which thread finished first. The M-step is serial. The block bootstrap \citep{kunsch1989} follows C psmc's: it cuts each sequence into blocks of 500,000 bins as \texttt{splitfa} does, a remainder shorter than 1.5 blocks staying in the last block, and each replicate draws blocks with replacement as C psmc's \texttt{psmc\_resamp} does, starting afresh from its own $\theta_0$. Replicates run in parallel, each drawing from its own ChaCha8 stream seeded from the bootstrap seed and its index. Posterior decoding (\opt{--tmrca-out}) gives, for every bin, the posterior mean TMRCA, the most probable state and the states at which the posterior reaches 2.5\% and 97.5\%.

\subsection*{Experiments}

All results come from one pipeline (\texttt{experiment/pipeline}) that simulates the genomes, runs both programs with matched settings, records how every output was made and draws every figure from its tables; Supplementary Note~1 describes how to reproduce them. We name the experiments E1--E7, as their directories in the repository are named. C psmc ran the command of its documentation, \texttt{psmc -N25 -t15 -r5 -p "4+25*2+4+6"}: 25 EM iterations, with the pattern and maximum time that \citet{li2011} used for human genomes. \psmcrs{} 0.2.0 ran the same settings with its own options. Both used 100~bp bins and one thread unless stated otherwise. Every seed was fixed in advance, from the SHA-256 of a string naming the experiment, model, replicate and stage.

\paragraph{Comparisons.} The fits of the two programs to the same input have the same intervals, whose boundaries differ in years only through $\theta$ and $t_{\max}$, and are compared interval by interval. For each interval $k$ of C psmc's fit that overlaps the window $[a,b]$, $d_k=\log_{10}(N^{\text{rs}}_k/N^{\text{C}}_k)$, where $N^{\text{rs}}_k$ and $N^{\text{C}}_k$ are the two fits' \Ne{} in interval $k$, weighted by $w_k=\ln(\min(e_k,b)/\max(s_k,a))$ for an interval from $s_k$ to $e_k$; their RMSE, $\Delta$, is $(\sum_kw_kd_k^2/\sum_kw_k)^{1/2}$. The window spans the 1\% to 99\% quantiles of the pairwise coalescence time under the true model (simulations) or under the fitted one (C psmc's where the programs are compared, \psmcrs{}'s otherwise). A cohort's window spans the medians, over its genomes, of these quantiles: for the 1000 Genomes cohort, \EsevenWindowLoKy{} thousand to \EsevenWindowHiMy{} million years ago. Fits of different inputs, whose $\theta$, and so whose time scales, differ, are compared at the same times (E4), except the VCF and \texttt{psmcfa} fits of a 1000 Genomes genome. These are compared interval by interval, as above, with $d_k=\log_{10}(N^{\text{VCF}}_k/N^{\text{psmcfa}}_k)$ on the \texttt{psmcfa} fit's intervals and window: the weighted mean $\bar d=\sum_kw_kd_k/\sum_kw_k$ is the shift between the two fits, and the weighted SD, $(\sum_kw_k(d_k-\bar d)^2/\sum_kw_k)^{1/2}$, the change of shape. A fit is compared with the truth by the RMSE of $\log_{10}\Ne$ over 200 log-spaced times in the window.

\paragraph{Simulated genomes (E1; Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}, Table~S1, Fig.~S1).} Four models, in diploid sizes and generations: constant size 10,000; a bottleneck (20,000 for 0--800 generations, 1,000 to 1,200, 10,000 to 4,000, 5,000 to 40,000, then 10,000); an expansion (10,000 for 0--400 generations, 1,000 to 2,400, 10,000 to 8,000, 5,000 to 40,000, 10,000 to 80,000, then 20,000); and the zigzag model of \citet{schiffels2014} from stdpopsim 0.3.0 \citep{adrion2020}. Each of \EoneReps{} replicates per model was \EoneChroms{} unlinked chromosomes of \EoneChromMb{}~Mb, simulated for one diploid individual with msprime 1.4.4 \citep{kelleher2016,baumdicker2022} under the coalescent with recombination, with $\mu=2.5\times10^{-8}$ and $r=10^{-8}$ per bp per generation, and scaled with $g=25$ years.

\paragraph{The residual difference (E1).} We traced the residual difference from C psmc on E1's \EoneGenomes{} genomes with builds of \psmcrs{} modified for this purpose, which are not part of the release (\texttt{experiment/\allowbreak c\_equivalence}). Each change described in Results was made alone: the last bin of each sequence was left out of the expected emission counts, as C psmc leaves it out, or the M-step was replaced by a port of C psmc's Hooke--Jeeves search. \psmcrs{}'s default fits were within a $\Delta$ of \DiagPrecisionMax{} (median \DiagPrecisionMedian{}) of fits whose M-steps ran to the limit of precision. The port of C psmc's search, run with the last bin also left out, was traced on an Apple M1 Pro laptop against C psmc's own search in the first M-step on the repository's test input: it evaluated the same parameters, bit for bit, until the two searches ranked differently two points whose objectives differed by less than the two programs' rounding.

\paragraph{Real genomes (E2; Fig.~\ref{fig:agree}c--e).} NA12878's \texttt{psmcfa} file is the one made for E7 (below). The \EtwoTurtlesW{} turtles are side-necked turtles (Pleurodira): \textit{Emydura subglobosa}, \textit{Hydromedusa tectifera} and \textit{Pelusios castaneus}. The turtle \texttt{psmcfa} files are those of \citet{hilgers2025}. The turtles were scaled with $\mu=4.6\times10^{-9}$, the mean of nine trios of the painted turtle \citep{bergeron2023}, and $g=15$ years, close to the generation times that \citet{sozzoni2025} used for two of the species; NA12878 with $\mu=1.25\times10^{-8}$ \citep{scally2012} and $g=29$ years \citep{fenner2005}. Each genome was checked with \opt{psmc-rs qc} and bootstrapped with \EtwoBootReps{} replicates on \EtwoBootThreads{} threads, in blocks of 50~Mb as \texttt{splitfa} cuts them (a sequence's last block keeps a remainder shorter than 1.5 blocks), which made every block of \textit{P.~castaneus} a whole scaffold. The turtles were also refitted with the pattern's first free $\lambda$ split into two (\opt{2+2+25*2+4+6}) or four (\opt{1+1+1+1+25*2+4+6}).

\paragraph{Performance (E3; Fig.~\ref{fig:perf}, Table~\ref{tab:timing}).} Genomes of 1, 3, 10 and 30 chromosomes of 100~Mb were simulated under constant size. C psmc ran on one thread and \psmcrs{} on 1, 8 and 30 threads, and also on 2, 4 and 16 threads on 3,000~Mb: \EthreeSetups{} setups of \EthreeRepeatsW{} repeats, each repeat on an exclusive \EthreeCpu{} node (\EthreeNodesW{} nodes in all). Before each run the node had to be quiet, with at most one core and 10\% of cores busy over 2~s; during the run, other processes could use at most 0.5 core and 5\% of cores, or the run was repeated later. Peak memory, in MB of $2^{20}$ bytes, is the larger of the program's \texttt{ru\_maxrss} and its process tree's resident memory sampled every 0.5~s. Outputs (C psmc's \texttt{.psmc}, \psmcrs{}'s JSON) were compared byte for byte with the same program's output on the fewest threads in the first repeat.

\paragraph{Partly callable bins, bootstrap and decoding (E4--E6; Figs S2 and S3).} E4 masked \EfourRepsW{} bottleneck genomes of E1's size with uncallable runs of mean \EfourClusRunKb{}~kb (clustered) or \EfourDispRunBp{}~bp (dispersed) covering 10\% or 30\% of positions. It compared \psmcrs{} on the VCF with its mask, with and without weighting; a consensus sequence converted by \texttt{fq2psmcfa}, which gave the unweighted fit exactly; multihetsep converted from the VCF and its mask; and the VCF without its mask, each against the fit of the same genome without missing data. E5 simulated \EfiveFits{} bottleneck genomes of \EfiveChroms{}$\times$50~Mb, fitted each, and bootstrapped \EfiveDatasets{} of them with \EfiveReps{} replicates, with blocks of 50 and 5~Mb. E6 read E1's first replicate of each model as \texttt{psmcfa}, as VCF and as multihetsep, and decoded E1's first bottleneck replicate with its fitted model (\opt{--tmrca-out} on 4 threads) against its true TMRCA, re-simulated from the recorded seeds.

\paragraph{1000 Genomes (E7; Fig.~\ref{fig:kg}).} The inputs were the joint-called VCFs of the 3,202 high-coverage samples \citep{byrskabishop2022} for chromosomes 1--22 (\EsevenRecords{} records), of which we used the \EsevenGenomes{} unrelated individuals; the GRCh38 strict accessibility mask \citep{kgp2015}; and, as a negative mask shared by all samples, the position of every record whose FILTER was neither PASS nor `.' (\EsevenNonpass{} records). Each chromosome was downloaded and checked against its published size and MD5 checksum, read in chunks of 15~Mb with \texttt{bcftools} 1.24 \citep{danecek2021} and split into one VCF per sample of its heterozygous or missing genotypes; \opt{psmc-rs convert --vcf-mode mask} then wrote each sample's \texttt{psmcfa}. For NA18507, NA19239 and NA12878, chromosome~\EsevenPilotChrom{} converted directly from the joint VCF gave files byte-identical to those made through the per-sample VCFs. Every genome was fitted from its \texttt{psmcfa}. The comparison subset, NA18507, NA19239, NA12878 and others drawn by seed to make two genomes per population (\EsevenDefault{} in all), was also fitted by C psmc, and from its VCFs with the masks and \opt{--bin-callable auto}. In each population, the first genome of the subset (NA18507 in YRI, NA12878 in CEU, elsewhere the first drawn) was also fitted with four free $\lambda$s in the four most recent intervals (\opt{1+1+1+1+25*2+4+6}), and NA18507, NA19239 and NA12878 were bootstrapped (\EsevenBootReps{} replicates on \EsevenBootThreads{} threads). Core-hours are the summed wall times of fits that ran on one thread each; C psmc's for the cohort are its median wall time per genome times \EsevenGenomes{}. Population and superpopulation curves are the medians of $\Ne$ across individuals, at each time of a common grid over the cohort's window. At each time, the populations' spread in a superpopulation is $\log_{10}$ of the highest over the lowest of its population medians, and its genomes' spread is $\log_{10}$ of the 90\% over the 10\% quantile of its genomes. We give the largest value of the populations' spread until the first free $\lambda$ has ended in each of the superpopulation's populations (at the median over the population's genomes). After that, we give medians over the grid times: of the populations' spread up to \EsevenPopCutKy{} thousand years ago and at older times, and of the genomes' spread at all times. For the comparison with Genome in a Bottle, NA12878's PASS records with a heterozygous genotype of single-base alleles were matched by position and alleles with the heterozygous single-nucleotide variants of HG001's GRCh38 v4.2.1 benchmark \citep{wagner2022} inside both the strict mask and the benchmark's regions (\EsevenGiabMb{}~Mb).

\paragraph{Software and computing.} The simulations and analyses used Python 3.13.13 with msprime 1.4.4, tskit 1.0.3, stdpopsim 0.3.0, NumPy 2.5.3, SciPy 1.18.1, pandas 3.0.6 and Matplotlib 3.11.2, and htslib and bcftools 1.24. \psmcrs{} 0.2.0 was built with rustc 1.99.0 and the release profile, without build flags; every \psmcrs{} fit on the cluster used the AVX2--FMA kernels (the laptop's refits, NEON; Supplementary Note~1, section~9). C psmc was lh3/psmc 0.6.5-r74, from sources identical to its commit 82fa2ad, with \texttt{fq2psmcfa} from the same sources, built with gcc 11.4.1 and \texttt{-O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -ffp-contract=off}, whose output was byte-identical to that of the Makefile's \texttt{-O2} build (Supplementary Note~1, section~7); \texttt{generate\_\allowbreak multihetsep.py} came from msmc-tools \citep{msmctools}. The fits ran on a computing cluster, on AMD EPYC 7702 nodes of 128 cores, and the figures were drawn from the tables on an Apple M1 Pro laptop. Every output has a provenance record of its command, settings, seeds, the checksums of its inputs and outputs, the identities of the tools and how the job ran.

\section*{Data availability}
The 1000 Genomes high-coverage VCFs are available from the International Genome Sample Resource (\wholeurl{https://www.internationalgenome.org}), the strict accessibility mask from the 1000 Genomes Project, and Genome in a Bottle's HG001 v4.2.1 benchmark from NIST. The inputs of the 1000 Genomes analysis, the \texttt{psmcfa} files of the \EsevenGenomes{} genomes, the comparison subset's VCFs and the masks, are available on Zenodo (\splitturl{https://doi.org/10.5281/}{zenodo.23764975}); the manifest of their sources, commands and checksums, every fit, bootstrap and table, and the turtle and NA12878 \texttt{psmcfa} files of E2 are in the repository (\texttt{experiment/runs}, \texttt{experiment/real\_data}). The turtle \texttt{psmcfa} files come from \citet{hilgers2025}.

\section*{Code availability}
\psmcrs{} is available at \wholeurl{https://github.com/larryivan/psmc-rs} under the MIT license; the release used here, \psmcrs{} 0.2.0, is archived on Zenodo (\splitturl{https://doi.org/10.5281/}{zenodo.23762893}). The experiment pipeline, its configuration, the committed results of every experiment and the code that draws every figure are in the same repository (\texttt{experiment/}); Supplementary Note~1 describes how to reproduce them. The numbers quoted in this article are generated from the committed results by \texttt{manuscript/make\_numbers.py}.
